lead: A datasheet value is a claim; a measurement is a fact. Attenuation is loss per kilometre. Dispersion is pulse spread per nanometre of source width per kilometre. Installers check both. Attenuation uses cutback or an OTDR. Dispersion uses pulse delay or phase shift. Only a few universities teach these measurements. The budgets in 5.2 and 5.3 depend on these numbers.
prereq: Unit 2 gives the physics. 5.2 and 5.3 show why α and D are needed.

blocks.text: Cutback compares output power from a long fiber with output power from a short piece. Source, launch and meter stay fixed. The difference is the loss of the removed piece.

items: Launch one fixed wavelength through a mode scrambler into the full length L₁.
Without moving source or launch, cut to a short length L₂ of a few metres.

blocks.where: α is attenuation in dB/km; L₁ and L₂ are long and short lengths in km; P₁ and P₂ are their output powers in the same unit.

blocks.text: P₂ is larger, so α is positive. Cutting keeps launch identical; a new connector would add its own loss.

An optical time-domain reflectometer (OTDR) sends a pulse and plots Rayleigh backscatter against distance. The trace falls at 2α per kilometre because the light travels out and back; the OTDR halves this, so the α it reports, and the slope of the display, is the one-way value in dB/km. Quiz readings are taken from that corrected display. A step down is splice or connector loss. A spike is reflection; its height gives reflectance. Dead zone is the blind stretch in metres after a strong reflection.
A splice reads differently from the two ends; average both directions for accuracy (see 5.5).

sections.h3: Dispersion in time and frequency domain

blocks.text: Time domain, also called pulse-delay or time-of-flight: send short pulses at several wavelengths, record arrival times, then plot group delay τ in ps against λ in nm. Its slope at the working wavelength gives dispersion.

blocks.where: D is dispersion in ps/(nm·km); L is fiber length in km; τ is group delay in ps; λ is wavelength in nm.

blocks.text: Frequency domain, or phase-shift method: modulate the source at f_m, sweep λ, read phase φ. A delay τ gives φ = 360° × f_m × τ, so τ = φ ÷ (360 f_m). No fast pulse detector is needed; production uses this method.

figure.caption: Only fiber length changes, so readings differ by the loss of the removed length.

spec.title: Cutback measurement of attenuation
spec.aria: Source through launch optics and 10 km fiber to a meter at 200 microwatts, then after cutting to 2 m a meter at 1000 microwatts, giving 0.6991 dB per km.

examples.question: A 1550 nm cutback measurement: with 10 km of fiber the meter reads 200 μW. The launch is untouched, the fiber is cut to 2 m, and the meter reads 1000 μW. (a) Find α. (b) Find total loss of the original 10 km.
steps: L₁ = 10 km, P₁ = 200 μW; L₂ = 2 m = 0.002 km, P₂ = 1000 μW.

This is much higher than the ~0.2 dB/km of modern single-mode fiber at 1550 nm, more like old or poor fiber. The arithmetic is what the question asks. An OTDR on the same fiber must show the same slope, 0.6991 dB/km.
examples.answer: α = 0.6991 dB/km (about 0.70 dB/km); 10 km of this fiber loses 6.99 dB.
examples.check:
import math
P1 = 200.0
P2 = 1000.0
L1 = 10.0
L2 = 0.002
loss = 10 * math.log10(P2 / P1)
alpha = loss / (L1 - L2)
print(round(loss, 4))
print(round(alpha, 4))
print(round(alpha * 10, 2))

examples.question: The same fiber in a pulse-delay (time-of-flight) dispersion set-up: relative group delay reads 500.0 ps at 1548 nm and 506.8 ps at 1552 nm over 10 km. Find D.
steps: This near-zero D at 1550 nm means the sample is dispersion-shifted fiber; ordinary single-mode fiber would show about 17 ps/(nm·km) here.
examples.answer: D = 0.17 ps/(nm·km); the sample is dispersion-shifted fiber.

traps: Dividing by total length L₁ instead of L₁ − L₂. The cut piece was not measured.
One reading in dBm and the other in μW, or lengths in metres. Use the same power unit and lengths in km.
Reading a splice straight after a connector spike. It sits in the dead zone.
Mixing units: α is dB/km, D is ps/(nm·km). 40 ps/nm on a 10 km spool is a total, not a coefficient; divide by 10 km to get 4 ps/(nm·km).
Confusing total loss in dB with the coefficient in dB/km.

quiz.q: What is the other name of the cutback method, and which two powers does it compare?
quiz.a: Two-point method. It compares output power at the long length with output power at a short cut-back length.

quiz.q: Why cut the fiber instead of disconnecting and rejoining it?
quiz.a: A new joint adds its own loss and changes the launch. Cutting keeps source, launch and meter identical.

quiz.q: OTDR markers at 2.0 km and 4.0 km on the corrected display differ by 1.2 dB. Find α.
Relative group delay is 500.0 ps at 1548 nm and 506.8 ps at 1552 nm over 10 km. Find D and name the fiber type.
quiz.a: dτ/dλ = 6.8 ps ÷ 4 nm = 1.7 ps/nm; D = 1.7 ÷ 10 km = 0.17 ps/(nm·km). This near-zero D means dispersion-shifted fiber.

quiz.q: A connector spike is followed by 8 m where nothing can be read. A splice sits 3 m after the connector. Can its loss be measured here?
quiz.a: No. It lies inside the dead zone. Measure from the far end and average the two directions.

quiz.q: Why does the phase-shift method avoid fast electronics?
quiz.a: Group delay is computed from phase, τ = φ ÷ (360 f_m). No picosecond pulse source or fast detector is needed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Field kits now combine an OTDR, a power meter and a fault locator in one handset. Search for 'OTDR dead zone', 'bidirectional OTDR splice loss' and 'modulation phase shift dispersion measurement'.
